title: Livery Stable Blues, Baquet and Yellow Nunez, and the Edwards lawsuit
summary: Laine's early band played its own compositions with funny names; he says Baquet and Yellow Nunez made up Livery Stable Blues, which Edwards took credit for in New York and Nunez sued over.

story.theme_name: Getting paid for records: royalties, publishing and flat fees
story.community_name: Royalties, publishing and who owns the song

blocks.x: Well, Papa, let me ask you this. What kind of music were you playing when you first started playing for money? What kind of music was it? Drums. Mm-hmm. Trap drums, a little bit alto, and bass fiddle. What kind of tunes did your band play?
What?
What kind of tunes did y'all play?
What kind of music? What kind of songs did you play?

What kind of songs? Mm-hmm. Well, all of our own composition. Your own composition? Yes. We had one man by the very, uh, Lawrence Vega and this part of Parquet. Well, in fact, the rest of them boys, they'd be with them all kinds of funny stuff. The first thing you know, when they'd get into the house with me and a bunch of kids, they'd want to try to see if they could play that stuff over again. Mm-hmm. And sure enough, they used us. Now, there was this Liberty Stable Blues, they call it. Liberty Stable Blues? Yeah. We, we, uh, Parquet composed that. Ah, S.H.I.E.L.D. Barquet, that one? Yes, sir. Yes, sir. Him and Yellow Nunez.
Mm-hmm.
Yes, sir. We used to call that, um, uh, let me tell you who's, we used to call that again. Yeah. Well, we had, we gave it different funny names.
I understand. I know, you told me about that before.
Yes.
Like florens and meatballs and numbers like that.

That's it, all that sort of stuff, see? Him give it different funny names, you know. So this fellow Edwards, goes up in New York. Mm-hmm. They've sent for me to go up there, and I wouldn't go up there because I had plenty of contracts down here, and I didn't want to go out of the city. I wanted to fill them contracts.
Papa, was this when you were 14? Was this when you were 14? Oh, no. No, this was later. That's later. Oh, later.
This was later.
This was in the 1910s. Oh, I see.

So anyhow, he got up there and he started to play. There wasn't such a thing during my time as records. There was nothing like that. Right. So he had this plowereen played, and he called it Liberty Stable Blues. Mm-hmm. And he took the credit for it. But that was brought in from Yellow Nunes and Bacquet.

Well, Yellow sued him, you know that. Yellow sued him. Yellow sued him. Tell him Yellow sued him. Yellow sued him. Took him to court. Yellow took him to court. Yellow. Oh, that song, yeah. Oh, yeah. He's dead. No, years ago. Years ago. He can't hear it. I don't know what you say.
Yellow sued Edwards for that on account of that same piece, you see, when he was up in New York.
Yeah.
Took him to court.
Don't you remember? I kind of remember. Yeah, Yellow sent and told us about it. Oh, yeah, they come to me. Yeah, Yellow told us, yeah.
That's it. They come to me. And I told them. Only two men. Yellow, Nunes, and Bacquet.
Yeah.
